title: Trump not concerned by WPS tensions, says issue will be 'taken care of'
summary: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he was not concerned about tensions in the West Philippine Sea, adding that the issue would be “taken care of.”

blocks.text: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he was not concerned about tensions in the West Philippine Sea, assuring that the issue would be “taken care of.”

"I'm not concerned at all. I'm not concerned about that at all. That'll be taken care of," Trump said when asked by a reporter how concerned he was about the maritime tensions and how prepared the United States was under its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) with the Philippines.

Trump made the remark during his bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang, where the two leaders reaffirmed their countries' longstanding alliance and discussed areas for greater cooperation.
The US president was in Manila on November 17 and 18 for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits.

During their opening remarks, Marcos described the United States as the Philippines' only treaty ally, noting that the two countries are marking 80 years of diplomatic relations and 75 years of their alliance under the MDT.

Trump, meanwhile, said the two countries were expanding their defense cooperation, citing increased US foreign military financing for the Philippines and the approval of more than US$5 billion (approximately P250 billion) in arms sales since he took office.
"America stands with the Filipino people just as we have for generations. We've been your ally, but not as close as it is now," Trump said.
The MDT, signed in 1951, commits the Philippines and the United States to come to each other's defense in the event of an armed attack on either country.
During the treaty's 75th anniversary, Washington reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the Philippines in monitoring its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and upholding its defense interests.
Tensions in the South China Sea have persisted amid China's expansive maritime claims, which overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.

On July 12, 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that China's sweeping claims over nearly the entire South China Sea had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Beijing has rejected the ruling.— MCG, GMA News
